questions.stem: An ideal Zener diode of breakdown voltage $8$ V is connected with an $800\ \Omega$ load and a $400\ \Omega$ series resistor across an $18$ V supply, as shown in the figure. Its power dissipation is
questions.solution:
In breakdown, $V_o=V_Z=8\text{ V}$. The series and load currents are
$$I_s=\frac{18-8}{400}=25\text{ mA},\qquad I_L=\frac{8}{800}=10\text{ mA}.$$
Hence $I_Z=I_s-I_L=15\text{ mA}$, so $P_Z=V_ZI_Z=8(15\text{ mA})=120\text{ mW}$.
questions.notes: figure check: The Zener diode is reversed: its cathode (the bar/hook end of the symbol) is drawn at the bottom toward the common return instead of at the output node, contradicting the brief (cathode at output node, anode at bottom).; The Zener diode label is missing the breakdown voltage: it is labeled only 'Zener' with no '8 V' value.; The output node label V_out is present but the bottom common-return 'Zener/common' labels overlap the wire/nodes slightly; 'Zener' text sits on the bottom wire.

questions.stem: A uniform horizontal rod of length $4$ m and mass $8$ kg is hinged at one end and held by a vertical string at the other. A $12$ kg load hangs $3$ m from the hinge. Find the string tension. Take $g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$.
questions.solution:
Taking moments about the hinge, the rod’s weight acts at its centre, $2$ m from the hinge.
$$4T=(8\times10)(2)+(12\times10)(3)=520$$
Hence, $T=130\,\text{N}$.

questions.stem: Charges $+16q$ and $-q$ are fixed on the $x$-axis at $x=-6$ cm and $x=18$ cm, respectively. The coordinate of the point where the electric field is zero is
questions.solution:
Between the charges, both electric fields point in the same direction, so the zero-field point lies outside; to the right, the fields oppose.
$$\frac{16}{(x+6)^2}=\frac{1}{(x-18)^2}\Rightarrow \frac{4}{x+6}=\frac{1}{x-18}\Rightarrow x=26\,\text{cm}$$

questions.stem: A transverse wave is described by $y(x,t)=0.03\sin(2\pi x-4\pi t)$, where $x$ and $y$ are in metres and $t$ is in seconds. Which set gives its amplitude, frequency, wavelength and speed, respectively?
questions.solution:
Comparing with $y=A\sin(kx-\omega t)$ gives $A=0.03\ \text{m}$, $k=2\pi\ \text{m}^{-1}$ and $\omega=4\pi\ \text{s}^{-1}$.
$$f=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}=2\ \text{Hz},\qquad \lambda=\frac{2\pi}{k}=1\ \text{m},\qquad v=\frac{\omega}{k}=2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$
Hence the set is $(0.03\ \text{m},\ 2\ \text{Hz},\ 1\ \text{m},\ 2\ \text{m s}^{-1})$.

questions.stem: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the screen is $1.6$ m from slits separated by $0.40$ mm, and the wavelength is $400$ nm. The amplitudes reaching the screen are in the ratio $1:2$. At the point where the path difference is $\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$, find its distance from the central maximum and its intensity relative to $I_{\max}$.
questions.solution: The fringe width is $[?]$

questions.stem: At the same temperature, the rms speed of methane molecules is $500$ m s$^{-1}$. Given molar masses of methane and helium as $16$ g mol$^{-1}$ and $4$ g mol$^{-1}$, respectively, the rms speed of helium molecules is:
questions.solution:
At the same temperature, $v_{\text{rms}} \propto 1/\sqrt{M}$. Thus,
$$v_{\text{He}}=500\sqrt{\frac{16}{4}}=1000\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$

questions.stem: A rigid vessel contains $4$ mol of an ideal monatomic gas. When $1992$ J of heat is supplied, the temperature of the gas rises by: (Take $R = 8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.)
questions.solution:
At constant volume, $W=0$, so $Q=nC_V\triangle T$, with $C_V=\frac{3}{2}R$ for a monatomic gas.
$$\triangle T=\frac{1992}{4\times\frac{3}{2}\times 8.3}=40\text{ K}$$

questions.stem: The position vector of a particle is $r(t)=(t^2+3t)i+(2t^2-t)j$ m, where $t$ is in seconds. What is its velocity at $t=2$ s?
questions.solution:
Velocity is the time derivative of position:
$$\vec v(t)=(2t+3)\mathbf i+(4t-1)\mathbf j.$$
At $t=2\,\mathrm{s}$, $\vec v=(7\mathbf i+7\mathbf j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

questions.stem: For a material in a weak applied field, the magnetization $M$ varies with field intensity $H$ as shown in the figure. Which class best describes the material?
questions.solution: The slope of the $M$–$H$ graph gives the magnetic susceptibility, $\chi=M/H$. Since the slope is negative, $\chi<0$, which is characteristic of a diamagnetic material.

questions.stem: A hydrogen-like lithium ion ($Z=3$) emits a photon when its electron moves from the $n=3$ level to the $n=2$ level. The energy of the photon is
questions.solution:
For a hydrogen-like ion, $E_n=-13.6Z^2/n^2$ eV, so the emitted photon energy is
$$E_\gamma=13.6(3)^2\left(\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{3^2}\right)=17.0\text{ eV}.$$

questions.stem: A particle of mass $2\ \text{kg}$ is at $(8,6)\ \text{m}$ relative to the origin and moves at $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the direction $3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}$. The magnitude of its angular momentum about the origin is:
questions.solution:
The velocity components are $\vec{v}=10\left(\frac{3}{5}\hat{i}+\frac{4}{5}\hat{j}\right)=(6\hat{i}+8\hat{j})\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so $\vec{p}=(12\hat{i}+16\hat{j})\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$.
$$|L_z|=|xp_y-yp_x|=|8(16)-6(12)|=56\ \text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$$

questions.stem: A radio wave travels through free space, where the speed of light is $3.0\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$. If its magnetic-field amplitude is $4.0\times10^{-8}$ T, what is its electric-field amplitude?
questions.solution:
For an electromagnetic wave in free space, $E_0=cB_0$.
$$E_0=(3.0\times10^8)(4.0\times10^{-8})=12\text{ V m}^{-1}$$

questions.stem: Two solid blocks float fully submerged across the same interface of two immiscible liquids. Block $P$ has $\dfrac{2}{3}$ of its volume in the upper liquid, while block $Q$ has $\dfrac{1}{3}$ there. If $\rho_P:\rho_Q=3:4$, find the ratio of the upper to lower liquid densities.
questions.solution:
For floating equilibrium, each block’s density equals the volume-weighted average liquid density:
$$\rho_P=\frac{2\rho_u+\rho_l}{3},\qquad \rho_Q=\frac{\rho_u+2\rho_l}{3}$$
Using $\rho_P/\rho_Q=3/4$, we get $4(2\rho_u+\rho_l)=3(\rho_u+2\rho_l)$, hence $\rho_u:\rho_l=2:5$.

questions.stem: In a Wheatstone bridge, a battery is connected across $A,C$ and a galvanometer across $B,D$. The arm resistances $AB,BC,CD,DA$ are respectively $a\parallel b$, $c+d$, $X+g$, and $e\parallel f$. All symbols denote resistances. If the bridge is balanced, what is $X$?
questions.solution:
At balance, $R_{AB}R_{CD}=R_{AD}R_{BC}$. Using $R_{AB}=\frac{ab}{a+b}$ and $R_{AD}=\frac{ef}{e+f}$,
$$X+g=\frac{\frac{ef}{e+f}(c+d)}{\frac{ab}{a+b}}=\frac{ef(c+d)(a+b)}{ab(e+f)}.$$
Hence, $X=\frac{ef(c+d)(a+b)}{ab(e+f)}-g$.

questions.stem: A radioactive nuclide has a half-life of $5$ h. What fraction of its initial nuclei remains undecayed after $15$ h?
questions.solution:
The number of half-lives elapsed is $n=15/5=3$.
$$\frac{N}{N_0}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3=\frac{1}{8}$$

questions.stem: Two long parallel wires, $20$ cm apart, carry currents of $3$ A and $6$ A in the same direction. A point lies on the line joining them, $10$ cm from the $3$ A wire on the side away from the other wire. The net magnetic field there is (take $\frac{\text{μ}_0}{2\text{π}}=2.0\times10^{-7}$ T m A$^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
The point lies outside both wires, so the magnetic fields add. Using $B=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\left(\dfrac{I_1}{r_1}+\dfrac{I_2}{r_2}\right)$, with $r_1=0.10$ m and $r_2=0.30$ m,
$$B=2.0\times10^{-7}\left(\frac{3}{0.10}+\frac{6}{0.30}\right)=1.0\times10^{-5}\text{ T}=10\,\mu\text{T}.$$

questions.stem: A $3\ \text{kg}$ block and a $6\ \text{kg}$ block are joined by a light string on a frictionless horizontal table. A horizontal force of $27\ \text{N}$ pulls the $3\ \text{kg}$ block away from the other block. What are the acceleration of the blocks and the string tension?
questions.solution:
For the two-block system, $a=\dfrac{F}{m_1+m_2}=\dfrac{27}{3+6}=3\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.
For the $6\ \text{kg}$ block, $T=m_2a=6(3)=18\ \text{N}$.

questions.stem: In a series $LCR$ circuit, the applied voltage leads the current by $60^\circ$. If the resistance is $10\ \Omega$, what is the impedance of the circuit?
questions.solution:
For a series $LCR$ circuit, $\cos\phi=R/Z$.
$$Z=\frac{R}{\cos60^\circ}=\frac{10}{1/2}=20\,\Omega$$

questions.stem: A $2\ \text{kg}$ block is at rest on a rough plane inclined at $45^\circ$. A horizontal force $F$ is applied as shown in the figure. If the coefficient of static friction is $\dfrac{1}{3}$, the range of $F$ for which the block remains in equilibrium is (take $g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$):
questions.solution:
The normal reaction is $N=\dfrac{mg+F}{\sqrt{2}}$, and equilibrium requires friction $\dfrac{|mg-F|}{\sqrt{2}}\leq\mu N$.
$$3|20-F|\leq 20+F$$
For $F\leq20$, this gives $F\geq10$; for $F\geq20$, it gives $F\leq40$. Thus, $10\ \text{N}\leq F\leq40\ \text{N}$.

questions.stem: A battery of emf $V$ remains connected to two series capacitors as shown in the figure. A dielectric completely fills $C_1$. What is the ratio of the voltage across $C_2$ to $V$?
questions.solution:
With the dielectric, $C_1=3C$ and $C_2=2C$. The series equivalent capacitance and charge are
$$C_{\rm eq}=\frac{(3C)(2C)}{3C+2C}=\frac{6C}{5},\qquad Q=C_{\rm eq}V=\frac{6CV}{5}.$$
Thus $V_2=Q/C_2=3V/5$, so $\dfrac{V_2}{V}=\boxed{\dfrac35}$.
questions.notes: figure check: Label mismatch: the lower capacitor is labelled C1 = C, while the 'C2 = 2C' label floats near the bottom wire with no capacitor next to it. The brief requires the upper capacitor to be C1 = C (with the dielectric slab, K = 3) and the lower capacitor to be C2 = 2C.; The dielectric slab is drawn floating to the left of the wires, not inside the gap of capacitor C1.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum has frequency $2$ Hz at one location. At another location, the acceleration due to gravity is $\frac{9}{16}$ of its original value. What is its frequency there?
questions.solution:
For the same pendulum length, $f \propto \sqrt{g}$. Thus,
$$f_2 = 2\sqrt{\frac{9}{16}} = \frac{3}{2}\text{ Hz}.$$

questions.stem: A vehicle covers two equal distances. Its speed over the first distance is $30$ km h$^{-1}$ and its average speed over the whole journey is $24$ km h$^{-1}$. Find its speed over the second distance.
questions.solution:
For equal distances, average speed is the harmonic mean of the two speeds:
$$24=\frac{2}{\frac{1}{30}+\frac{1}{v}}$$
Thus, $\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{12}-\frac{1}{30}=\frac{1}{20}$, so $v=20$ km h$^{-1}$.

questions.stem: A wire of length $L$ and radius $r$ extends by $x$ under load $F$. A wire of the same material, length $2L$ and radius $2r$, is subjected to load $6F$. Its extension is
questions.solution:
For the same material, extension is $\Delta L=\dfrac{FL}{AY}$. Thus,
$$x_2=\frac{(6F)(2L)}{\pi(2r)^2Y}=3\frac{FL}{\pi r^2Y}=3x$$

questions.stem: A circular conducting loop lies in a uniform magnetic field of $0.2\ \text{T}$ perpendicular to its plane. Its radius is increasing at $5\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$; at the instant its radius is $10\ \text{cm}$, as shown in the figure. The induced emf is
questions.solution:
By Faraday’s law, $\mathcal{E}=|d\triangle\text{Phi}/dt|=B\,d(\pi r^2)/dt=2\pi Br\,dr/dt$.
$$\mathcal{E}=2\pi(0.2)(0.10)(0.05)=0.002\pi\ \text{V}=2\pi\ \text{mV}$$

questions.stem: Two non-relativistic particles of masses $m$ and $4m$ have equal kinetic energies. What is the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths, $\dfrac{\lambda_m}{\lambda_{4m}}$?
questions.solution: For equal kinetic energy, $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\propto m^{-1/2}$. Thus, $$\dfrac{\lambda_m}{\lambda_{4m}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{4m}{m}}=2.$$
questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

questions.stem: The dimensionless Ohnesorge number is $Oh=\dfrac{\eta}{\sqrt{\rho\sigma d}}$, where $\eta$ is dynamic viscosity, $\rho$ is density, and $d$ is a length. What is the dimensional formula of $\sigma$?
questions.solution:
Since $Oh$ is dimensionless, $[\text{σ}]=[η]^2/([ρ][d])$.
$$[\text{σ}]=\frac{[M L^{-1}T^{-1}]^2}{[M L^{-3}][L]}=[M L^0T^{-2}]$$

questions.stem: A $4\ \text{kg}$ body moving at $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ collides head-on with a $2\ \text{kg}$ body moving at $3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the opposite direction. They stick together. Their common velocity and the loss in kinetic energy are, respectively,
questions.solution:
Taking the 4 kg body's direction as positive, conservation of momentum gives
$$v=\frac{4(3)-2(3)}{4+2}=1\ \text{m s}^{-1}.$$
Initial kinetic energy is $27\ \text{J}$ and final kinetic energy is $\frac12(6)(1)^2=3\ \text{J}$; hence the loss is $27-3=24\ \text{J}$.

questions.stem: Assuming the Earth has uniform density, what is the ratio of $g$ at a height $R$ above its surface to $g$ at a depth $R/2$ below its surface, where $R$ is the Earth's radius?
questions.solution:
At height $R$, $g_h=g\left(\dfrac{R}{R+R}\right)^2=\dfrac{g}{4}$. For a uniform-density Earth, at depth $R/2$, $g_d=g\left(1-\dfrac{R/2}{R}\right)=\dfrac{g}{2}$.
$$g_h:g_d=\dfrac{g}{4}:\dfrac{g}{2}=1:2$$

questions.stem: Water of mass $M$ at $T^\circ\text{C}$ is added to $m$ ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$ in an insulated calorimeter of heat capacity $C$, initially at $0^\circ\text{C}$. If all the ice melts and the final temperature is above zero, find it. The specific heat of water is $s$ and the latent heat of fusion is $L$.
questions.solution:
By conservation of heat, heat lost by water equals heat used to melt the ice and warm the melted ice and calorimeter:
$$Ms(T-T_f)=mL+(ms+C)T_f$$
Rearranging gives $T_f=\dfrac{MsT-mL}{(M+m)s+C}$.

questions.stem: A thin converging lens of refractive index $1.60$ has power $+5.0\ \text{D}$ in air. It is immersed in a liquid of refractive index $1.20$. What are its focal length and nature?
questions.solution:
The power of a lens in a medium is $P_m=P_a\dfrac{(n_l/n_m)-1}{n_l-1}$.
$$P_m=5.0\dfrac{(1.60/1.20)-1}{1.60-1}=\frac{25}{9}\,\text{D},\qquad f_m=\frac{1}{P_m}=+0.36\,\text{m}=+36\,\text{cm}$$
Since the focal length is positive, the lens remains converging.

questions.stem: Three of the following species have trigonal planar molecular geometry. Which species is the odd one out?
questions.solution:
By VSEPR theory, $\text{BF}_3$, $\text{NO}_3^-$, and $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ are $AX_3$ species with trigonal planar geometry.
$\text{NH}_3$ is $AX_3E$; its lone pair gives it a trigonal pyramidal geometry, so it is the odd one out.

questions.stem: Which of the following orders of first ionisation enthalpy is incorrect?
questions.solution:
Across a period, first ionisation enthalpy generally increases, but boron has a lower value than beryllium due to its higher-energy $2p$ electron.
$$I_1(\text{Li}) < I_1(\text{B}) < I_1(\text{Be}) < I_1(\text{C})$$
Hence the order in (D) is incorrect.

questions.stem: Which aqueous ion characteristically forms a blue solution due to transitions within a partially filled $d$ subshell?
questions.solution:
Aqueous $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ has a partially filled $3d^9$ subshell, allowing $d$–$d$ transitions that produce its characteristic blue colour.
Thus, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ forms a blue solution.

questions.stem: Identify the final product $X$ in the two-step sequence shown in the figure.
questions.solution:
Phenol forms sodium phenoxide with NaOH; phenoxide then undergoes Williamson ether synthesis with methyl iodide.
$$\mathrm{C_6H_5ONa + CH_3I \rightarrow C_6H_5OCH_3 + NaI}$$
Thus, $X$ is methoxybenzene.

questions.stem: Consider these statements about xenon fluorides and their hydrolysis. How many are correct? I. In $\text{XeF}_2$, three equatorial lone pairs give a linear shape and $sp^3d$ hybridisation. II. $\text{XeF}_4$ is square planar with two opposite lone pairs and $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation. III. $\text{XeF}_6$ is distorted octahedral; its controlled hydrolysis can give square-pyramidal $\text{XeOF}_4$, see-saw $\text{XeO}_2\text{F}_2$, and finally $\text{XeO}_3$, with xenon remaining in the $+6$ oxidation state. IV. Complete hydrolysis of $\text{XeF}_2$ gives xenon and oxygen in a $1:1$ molar ratio, besides HF.
questions.solution:
For XeF₂, XeF₄ and XeF₆, the stated shapes, hybridisations and controlled hydrolysis products in I–III are correct; xenon remains at $+6$ in the XeF₆ hydrolysis sequence.
$$2\text{XeF}_2+2\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow2\text{Xe}+\text{O}_2+4\text{HF}$$
Thus $n(\text{Xe}):n(\text{O}_2)=2:1$, so IV is false. Three statements are correct.

questions.stem: Which description correctly gives the numbers, locations and surrounding atoms of the two types of voids in an fcc unit cell?

options.text: 8 tetrahedral voids at the centres of the eight smaller cubes, each surrounded by 4 atoms; 1 octahedral void at the body centre only, surrounded by 6 atoms.
8 tetrahedral voids at the centres of the eight smaller cubes, each surrounded by 6 atoms; 4 octahedral voids at the body centre and edge centres, each surrounded by 4 atoms.
8 tetrahedral voids at the centres of the eight smaller cubes, each surrounded by 4 atoms; 4 octahedral voids at the body centre and edge centres, each surrounded by 6 atoms.
8 tetrahedral voids at the centres of the eight smaller cubes, each surrounded by 4 atoms; 13 octahedral voids at the body centre and all twelve edge centres, each surrounded by 6 atoms.

questions.solution: Tetrahedral voids lie at the centres of the eight smaller cubes, each surrounded by 4 atoms. Octahedral voids: $1+\frac{12}{4}=4$ per unit cell, at the body centre and edge centres; each is surrounded by 6 atoms.

questions.stem: Which option identifies the radical released by CFC photolysis, its ozone-depletion cycle, and the role of $\text{NO}_x$ correctly?

options.text: CFC photolysis releases $\dot{\text{Cl}}$; $\dot{\text{Cl}}+\text{O}_3\rightarrow\text{Cl}\dot{\text{O}}+\text{O}_2$, then $\text{Cl}\dot{\text{O}}+\text{O}_2\rightarrow\dot{\text{Cl}}+\text{O}_3$; $\text{NO}$ is regenerated in a separate catalytic cycle.

CFC photolysis releases $\dot{\text{Cl}}$; $\dot{\text{Cl}}+\text{O}_3\rightarrow\text{Cl}\dot{\text{O}}+\text{O}_2$, then $\text{Cl}\dot{\text{O}}+\text{O}\rightarrow\dot{\text{Cl}}+\text{O}_2$; $\text{NO}$ is regenerated in a separate catalytic cycle.

CFC photolysis releases $\text{Cl}\dot{\text{O}}$; $\dot{\text{Cl}}+\text{O}_3\rightarrow\text{Cl}\dot{\text{O}}+\text{O}_2$, then $\text{Cl}\dot{\text{O}}+\text{O}\rightarrow\dot{\text{Cl}}+\text{O}_2$; $\text{NO}$ is regenerated in a separate catalytic cycle.

CFC photolysis releases $\dot{\text{Cl}}$; $\dot{\text{Cl}}+\text{O}_3\rightarrow\text{Cl}\dot{\text{O}}+\text{O}_2$, then $\text{Cl}\dot{\text{O}}+\text{O}\rightarrow\dot{\text{Cl}}+\text{O}_2$; unlike chlorine radicals, $\text{NO}$ is consumed stoichiometrically and is not regenerated from $\text{NO}_2$.

questions.solution:
CFC photolysis releases $\dot{Cl}$, which is regenerated in the catalytic cycle:
$$\dot{Cl}+O_3\rightarrow Cl\dot{O}+O_2,\qquad Cl\dot{O}+O\rightarrow\dot{Cl}+O_2$$
Similarly, $NO$ is regenerated in the separate cycle $NO+O_3\rightarrow NO_2+O_2$ and $NO_2+O\rightarrow NO+O_2$. Thus, option (B).

questions.stem: The alkene shown undergoes ozonolysis followed by reductive workup with $\text{Zn}/\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The products are:
questions.solution:
Reductive ozonolysis cleaves the C=C bond; a carbon bearing two carbon groups forms a ketone, while one bearing H forms an aldehyde.
$$\text{CH}_3\text{C(CH}_3)=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{O}_3,\,\text{Zn}/\text{H}_2\text{O}} \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$$
The products are propanone and propanal.

questions.stem: For an isolated gaseous $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ion ($Z=27$), what are its $d$-electron configuration, number of unpaired electrons and spin-only magnetic moment, respectively?
questions.solution:
Co has configuration $[\text{Ar}]3d^7 4s^2$; removing the two $4s$ electrons gives $\text{Co}^{2+}: [\text{Ar}]3d^7$. Hund’s rule gives $n=3$ unpaired electrons.
$$\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}=\sqrt{3(5)}=\sqrt{15}\ \text{BM}$$

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of $4\ \text{min}$. How long does the reactant concentration take to fall from $0.80$ to $0.10\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$?
questions.solution:
For a first-order reaction, each half-life halves the concentration. Since $\dfrac{0.10}{0.80}=\dfrac18=\left(\dfrac12\right)^3$, this takes three half-lives.
$$t=3(4)=12\ \text{min}$$

questions.stem: For the reaction $\text{PCl}_5(g) \rightarrow \text{PCl}_3(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$, $\Delta U = 87.0000\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ at $300\ \text{K}$. Find $\Delta H$. Take $R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$.
questions.solution: For ideal gases, $[?]$

questions.stem: The molar solubility of $\text{A}_2\text{B}$ is $3.0\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$. For $\text{A}_2\text{B}(s)\rightleftharpoons 2\text{A}^+(aq)+\text{B}^{2-}(aq)$, the value of $K_{\text{sp}}$ is:
questions.solution:
For molar solubility $s$, $[\text{A}^+]=2s$ and $[\text{B}^{2-}]=s$.
$$K_{\text{sp}}=[\text{A}^+]^2[\text{B}^{2-}]=4s^3=4(3.0\times10^{-4})^3=1.08\times10^{-10}\ \text{mol}^3\text{L}^{-3}$$

questions.stem: The apparent molar mass of $\text{K}_3[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$ in dilute solution is $164.5$ g mol$^{-1}$; its true molar mass is $329$ g mol$^{-1}$. What is its degree of dissociation?
questions.solution:
The van’t Hoff factor is $i=\dfrac{M}{M_{\mathrm{app}}}=\dfrac{329}{164.5}=2$. Since $\mathrm{K_3[Fe(CN)_6]}$ dissociates into 4 ions, $i=1+3\alpha$.
$$2=1+3\alpha\implies \alpha=\frac{1}{3}=33\dfrac{1}{3}\%$$

questions.stem: The ether-forming step in Williamson synthesis is usually an $S_\mathrm{N}2$ reaction. Why are aryl and vinyl halides unsuitable substrates for this step?

options.text: The carbon bonded to X is $sp^2$-hybridised; the C–X bond has partial double-bond character, hindering backside attack.
Ionisation of the C–X bond readily forms a resonance-stabilised aryl or vinyl carbocation, favouring $S_\mathrm{N}1$.
They lack a β-hydrogen, so the alkoxide cannot begin the substitution by removing a proton.
Alkoxide ions are too weak as nucleophiles to displace halide ions from carbon.

questions.solution: Williamson ether synthesis proceeds by backside $S_\mathrm{N}2$ attack. In aryl and vinyl halides, the C–X bond is attached to an $sp^2$-hybridised carbon and has partial double-bond character, hindering this attack.

questions.stem: The increasing order of stability of the following carbanions is: (I) benzyl, (II) allyl, (III) methyl, (IV) tert-butyl.
questions.solution:
Alkyl groups destabilize carbanions, so methyl is more stable than tert-butyl. Resonance stabilizes allyl and benzyl carbanions, with greater stabilization for benzyl.
Thus, the increasing order of stability is $\text{IV} < \text{III} < \text{II} < \text{I}$.

questions.stem: What is the configuration at the stereocentre, and what configuration results from rotating the Fischer projection by $180^\circ$ in the plane? Use the figure.
questions.solution:
CIP priority order is $$OH $>$ NH₂ $>$ COOH $>$ CH₂OH$$. With the lowest-priority group directed away, $1\to2\to3$ is clockwise, giving $(R)$.
A $180^\circ$ in-plane rotation of a Fischer projection preserves configuration; it remains $(R)$.

questions.stem: Cimetidine is used mainly for which therapeutic purpose?

options.text: Relief of mild to moderate pain

questions.solution: Cimetidine blocks histamine H$_2$ receptors in the stomach wall, reducing gastric acid secretion. It is used to treat peptic ulcers.

questions.stem: On heating glucose with excess phenylhydrazine, yellow needle-shaped crystals form. This observation identifies which carbohydrate test?
questions.solution:
On heating, glucose reacts with excess phenylhydrazine to form yellow crystalline osazone.
This characteristic crystal formation identifies the osazone test.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the weakest base in aqueous solution?
questions.solution: In aniline, the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton. Hence, aniline is the weakest base in aqueous solution.

questions.stem: Two ideal gases A and B have equal densities when A is at pressure $2P$ and temperature $3T$, and B is at pressure $3P$ and temperature $2T$. What is $\dfrac{\rho_A}{\rho_B}$ when A is at pressure $3P$ and temperature $2T$, while B is at pressure $2P$ and temperature $3T$?
questions.solution:
For an ideal gas, $\rho\propto PM/T$. Equal initial densities give
$$\frac{2M_A}{3T}=\frac{3M_B}{2T}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{M_A}{M_B}=\frac{9}{4}.$$
Thus, in the requested states, $\dfrac{\rho_A}{\rho_B}=\dfrac{M_A}{M_B}\dfrac{3/2}{2/3}=\dfrac{9}{4}\cdot\dfrac{9}{4}=\boxed{\dfrac{81}{16}}$.

questions.stem: At $298\ \text{K}$, a hydrogen electrode has pH $2$ and hydrogen pressure $1\ \text{bar}$. Find its reduction potential. Take $E^\circ=0\ \text{V}$ and $2.303RT/F=0.059\ \text{V}$.
questions.solution:
For $2\mathrm{H}^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2$, the Nernst equation is
$$E=E^\circ-\frac{0.059}{2}\log\left(\frac{P_{\mathrm{H}_2}}{[\mathrm{H}^+]^2}\right).$$
Using $P_{\mathrm{H}_2}=1$ bar and $[\mathrm{H}^+]=10^{-2}$, $E=-\frac{0.059}{2}\log(10^4)=-0.118\ \text{V}$.

questions.stem: The ester shown is treated with $2$ equivalents of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{MgBr}$ followed by dilute $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$. Which product is formed?
questions.solution:
An ester reacts with $2$ equivalents of a Grignard reagent to form a tertiary alcohol after hydrolysis; the alkoxy group is displaced during the first addition.
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow[\text{then }\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]{2\,\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{MgBr}} (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3\text{COH}$$
The product is 3-ethylpentan-3-ol.

questions.stem: The correct IUPAC name of the coordination compound $\text{K}_2[\text{PtCl}_6]$ is
questions.solution:
Let the oxidation state of Pt be $x$. For $[\text{PtCl}_6]^{2-}$,
$$x+6(-1)=-2 \Rightarrow x=+4.$$
The anionic complex uses the suffix “-ate”; six chlorido ligands give hexachlorido. Hence the name is potassium hexachloridoplatinate(IV).

questions.stem: How many unpaired electrons are present in tetrahedral $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$? (Atomic number of Ni = 28)
questions.solution:
For $[\text{NiCl}_4]^{2-}$, the oxidation state of Ni is $x-4=-2$, so $x=+2$ and Ni$^{2+}$ is $3d^8$.
In a tetrahedral field, the configuration is $e^4t_2^4$; hence it has $2$ unpaired electrons.

questions.stem: At $298\ \text{K}$, a cell reaction transfers $2$ mol of electrons and has $E^\circ_\text{cell}=+0.0592\ \text{V}$. Find its equilibrium constant $K$. Take $2.303RT/F=0.0592\ \text{V}$.
questions.solution:
For a cell reaction, $
\log_{10}K=\dfrac{nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}}{2.303RT}=\dfrac{2(0.0592)}{0.0592}=2$.
Hence, $K=10^2=100$.

questions.stem: Which reaction is expected to give a racemic substitution product at the carbon bearing the leaving group?

options.text: 2-bromobutane reacting with sodium azide in dimethyl sulfoxide
Optically pure 1-chloro-1-phenylethane undergoing solvolysis in aqueous ethanol
1-bromobutane reacting with sodium cyanide in dimethyl sulfoxide
2-bromobutane reacting with sodium iodide in acetone

questions.solution:
Solvolysis of optically pure 1-chloro-1-phenylethane forms a resonance-stabilized, planar benzylic carbocation.
$$\text{Ph–CH(Cl)–CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{Ph–C}^+\text{H–CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{attack from either face}} \text{racemic substitution product}$$
Thus, substitution at the chiral carbon gives a nearly racemic product.

questions.stem: What volume of $0.30\ \text{M}$ KOH is needed to completely neutralise $30\ \text{mL}$ of $0.20\ \text{M}$ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$?
questions.solution:
The reaction is $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4+2\text{KOH}\rightarrow\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4+2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, so $2$ mol of KOH neutralise $1$ mol of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
$$V_{\text{KOH}}=\frac{2(0.20)(30)}{0.30}=40\text{ mL}$$

questions.stem: In a hydrogen atom, an electron cascades from $n=5$ through $n=3$ to $n=2$. If the wavelength of the $4\to2$ line is $\lambda$, what is the total energy of the two emitted photons?
questions.solution:
The total energy emitted in the cascade equals the energy difference for the transition $5\to2$.
$$E=hcR_H\left(\frac14-\frac1{25}\right),\qquad \frac{hc}{\lambda}=hcR_H\left(\frac14-\frac1{16}\right)$$
Thus, $\dfrac{E}{hc/\lambda}=\dfrac{21/100}{3/16}=\dfrac{28}{25}$, so $E=\dfrac{28}{25}\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$.

questions.stem: Which of the cyclic species labelled I–IV in the figure are aromatic according to Hückel’s rule?
questions.solution:
A planar cyclic conjugated species is aromatic if it has $4n+2$ π electrons. I and II each have $6π$ electrons ($n=1$), so both are aromatic; III has $4π$ electrons and IV is non-planar.
Thus, I and II only.

questions.stem: Although the scholarship scheme was initially praised as ___, later audits revealed its ___ effects on applicants from rural areas.
questions.solution: The contrast is between the scheme’s initial reputation and the later audit findings. It was praised as <u>inclusive</u>, but its effects were <u>exclusionary</u> for rural applicants.

questions.stem:
In the sentence below, find the part that contains an error in subject–verb agreement.
**(A)** The collection of rare manuscripts
**(B)** in the university library
**(C)** are being catalogued
**(D)** by a team of trained archivists.

options.text: by a team of trained archivists.

questions.solution: The subject is the singular noun “collection”; the intervening phrase “of rare manuscripts” does not affect subject–verb agreement. The verb should be “is being catalogued,” not “are being catalogued.”

questions.stem: During her first week at the firm, Meera **learned the ropes** by observing her experienced colleagues. What does the idiom mean?

options.text: Took charge of the entire department
Understood how to perform the necessary tasks
Changed the rules of the workplace

questions.solution: “Learn the ropes” means becoming familiar with how a job or activity is done. By observing her colleagues, Meera understood how to perform the necessary tasks.

questions.stem: The librarian asked visitors to remain ______ so that other readers could study without disturbance.
questions.solution: “Silent” means making no noise, allowing other readers to study without disturbance.

questions.stem:
Choose the word which is nearest in meaning to the given word.

**GAINSAY**
questions.solution: “Gainsay” means to deny or contradict a statement; hence, “contradict” is the closest meaning.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences should be the opening sentence of a coherent paragraph formed by them?

options.text: As a result, the practice can help reduce the amount of waste sent to landfills.
This material can then be added to gardens to improve the soil.
Composting turns organic waste, such as food scraps and dry leaves, into a nutrient-rich material.
The process also gives households a practical way to manage biodegradable refuse.

questions.solution: (C) introduces composting and explains what it produces, so it provides the context needed for the later references to “this material” and “the process.”

questions.stem:
In the sentence given below, find the part that contains an error.
**(A)** The delegates **(B)** discussed about the revised timetable **(C)** before submitting their recommendations **(D)** to the chairperson.
questions.solution: “Discuss” takes a direct object and is not followed by “about” here. The sentence should read “discussed the revised timetable.”

questions.stem:
Choose the word opposite in meaning to the word given in capital letters.

**SCARCE**
questions.solution: “Scarce” means available in small quantity; “abundant” means available in large quantity, making it the opposite. Limited, rare, and insufficient are similar in meaning to scarce.

questions.stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

In many cities, rainwater is treated chiefly as a problem to be removed quickly. Drains and concrete channels carry it away, but heavy downpours can overwhelm these systems and send water into streets and homes. Urban wetlands offer a different approach. These low-lying areas, where water collects temporarily, can absorb rainfall and slow its movement across the land. Their plants and soils also filter some pollutants before water reaches rivers or underground supplies.

Wetlands do not eliminate the need for drains, nor can they prevent every flood. Their effectiveness depends on their size, location, and condition. A wetland that has been filled or cut off from its natural water flows may provide little protection. For this reason, planners increasingly consider wetlands as part of a broader network that includes pipes, parks, and other green spaces.

The benefits extend beyond water management. Wetlands provide habitat for birds and insects, and they can offer residents places for recreation and contact with nature. Protecting them may therefore serve several public purposes at once. Yet these benefits are easily overlooked when land is valued only for immediate construction. Recognising wetlands as working urban infrastructure does not mean that every wet area should remain untouched; it means that decisions about development should account for the services these landscapes provide, as well as the costs of replacing them.

What is the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Urban wetlands can replace conventional drainage systems if they are protected from development.
The main value of urban wetlands lies in providing recreation and wildlife habitat.
Cities should prevent all construction on low-lying land to avoid flooding and pollution.
Wetlands serve several urban functions and should be considered in development decisions.

questions.solution: The passage presents wetlands as serving multiple purposes: managing water, supporting wildlife, and providing recreation. It concludes that these services should be considered when making development decisions.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a wetland that has been disconnected from its natural water flows?

options.text: It will usually filter pollutants more effectively than a connected wetland.
It may be less effective at absorbing rainfall and reducing flood risk.
It will provide habitat but no benefits related to water management.
It can compensate for the loss of nearby drains and green spaces.

questions.solution: A wetland disconnected from its natural water flows may provide little protection, so it may be less effective at absorbing rainfall and reducing flood risk.

questions.stem: Find the next term in the following $\alpha-numeric$ series: C4X, G9T, K16P, O25L, ?
questions.solution:
The first letters advance by 4: C, G, K, O, S. The numbers are consecutive squares, so the next is $6^2=36$.
The last letters retreat by 4: X, T, P, L, H. Hence, the next term is S36H.

Arrange the following words in the order in which they appear in an English dictionary.

2. Game
3. Gate
4. Gave
questions.solution: All words begin with “Ga”; compare the third letters: $m<t<v<z$. Hence the dictionary order is Game, Gate, Gave, Gaze, i.e. $2,3,4,1$.

questions.stem:
Read the statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming the statements are true, determine which conclusions follow.

**Statements:**
All lanterns are instruments.
All instruments are portable.

**Conclusions:**
I. All lanterns are portable.
II. Some portable things are instruments.
III. All portable things are lanterns.
IV. No lantern is portable.
questions.solution: Lanterns ⊆ instruments ⊆ portable things, so I follows by transitivity. Since instruments exist under the standard syllogism convention, II follows. III reverses the inclusion, while IV contradicts I.

questions.stem: In a certain code language, “ra ki mo” means “birds build nests”, “zu ki fe” means “children build kites”, and “ra do pa” means “birds fly high”. What is the code for “birds”?
questions.solution: The first and third phrases share only the word “birds”; their only common code is “ra”. Hence, birds = ra.

questions.stem: Pointing to a boy, Leena said, “His father is the only son of my maternal grandfather.” How is the boy related to Leena?
questions.solution: Leena’s maternal grandfather’s only son is her maternal uncle. The boy is her maternal uncle’s son, so he is her cousin.

questions.stem: In a certain code, each letter is shifted forward by 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 places successively. If **MANGO** is coded as **NCQKT**, how will **TABLE** be coded?
questions.solution:
The letters are shifted forward successively by $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ places.
$T\to U,\ A\to C,\ B\to E,\ L\to P,\ E\to J$
Hence, TABLE is coded as UCEPJ.

questions.stem: Meera and Nisha are sisters. Meera has one son and one daughter; Nisha has two daughters and one son. How many female first cousins does Meera’s son have?
questions.solution: Meera’s son’s first cousins are Nisha’s children. Since Nisha has two daughters, he has $2$ female first cousins.

questions.stem:
Which set of letters, inserted in order at the blanks, completes the repeating letter series?

m _ o m n _ m _ o m _ o m n _
questions.solution:
The series repeats the block $mno$:
$mno \mid mno \mid mno \mid mno \mid mno$.
Thus, the missing letters in order are $n, o, n, n, o$.

questions.stem: Given **ACE : 1-6-15**, select the number group related to **BDF** by the same rule.
questions.solution:
Multiply each letter’s alphabet position by its place in the group: $A,C,E \to 1×1, 3×2, 5×3 = 1-6-15$.
Thus, $B,D,F \to 2×1, 4×2, 6×3 = 2-8-18$.

questions.stem:
Consider the statements to be true and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

**Statements:**
All falcons are birds.
Some falcons are nocturnal.
Some falcons are not nocturnal.
No nocturnal bird is silent.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some falcons being silent is a possibility.
II. All falcons being silent is a possibility.
questions.solution: Some falcons are not nocturnal, and they could be silent; hence I is possible. Some falcons are nocturnal, and since all falcons are birds, these falcons cannot be silent; hence II is impossible.

questions.stem: Three of the following four letter-number pairs follow the same rule. Choose the pair that does not fit.
questions.solution: The number equals the alphabetical position of the first letter plus 2: $B=2\to4$, $C=3\to5$, and $H=8\to10$. For MOP, $M=13$, so the number should be $15$, not $12$.

questions.stem: The value of $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1-\cos(7x)}{1-\cos(2x)}$ is
questions.solution:
Using $1-\cos u\sim \dfrac{u^2}{2}$ as $u\to0$,
$$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos(7x)}{1-\cos(2x)}=\frac{(7x)^2/2}{(2x)^2/2}=\frac{49}{4}.$$

questions.stem: How many skew-symmetric $3\times3$ matrices have every entry in $S=\{-4,-2,0,2,4,5\}$?
questions.solution:
For a skew-symmetric matrix, $A^T=-A$, so all diagonal entries are $0$. Each of the three independent upper-triangular entries must have its negative in $S$, giving $5$ choices: $-4,-2,0,2,4$.
$$5^3=125$$

questions.stem: For $a>0$ and $|r|<1$, if $\log_3(a+ar+ar^2+\cdots)=1+\log_3 a$, then the common ratio $r$ is
questions.solution:
The infinite geometric series sums to $\frac{a}{1-r}$. Since $1+\log_3 a=\log_3(3a)$,
$$\frac{a}{1-r}=3a \implies r=\frac{2}{3}.$$

questions.stem: If $z$ satisfies $\arg\left(\dfrac{z+3-2i}{z-5-6i}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, then its locus is
questions.solution:
Let $z=x+iy$. Since the quotient has argument $\pi/2$, $(z+3-2i)\overline{(z-5-6i)}$ has zero real part and positive imaginary part:
$$ (x+3)(x-5)+(y-2)(y-6)=0 \implies (x-1)^2+(y-4)^2=20. $$
Its imaginary part is $4(x-2y+7)>0$, so the locus is $|z-(1+4i)|=2\sqrt5$ with $\operatorname{Re}z-2\operatorname{Im}z+7>0$.

questions.stem: Let $[t]$ denote the greatest integer not exceeding $t$. For $-3\le x<3$, the values excluded from the range of $f(x)=[x]^2+2(x-[x])$ are
questions.solution:
Write $x=n+t$, where $n=[x]\in\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2\}$ and $0\le t<1$. Then $f(x)=n^2+2t\in[n^2,n^2+2)$.
Hence the range is $[0,3)\cup[4,6)\cup[9,11)$, so the excluded values are $(-\infty,0)\cup[3,4)\cup[6,9)\cup[11,\infty)$.

questions.stem: A committee of $8$ is chosen from $10$ men and $8$ women. How many committees have at least $3$ and at most $5$ women?
questions.solution:
For $w$ women, the remaining $8-w$ members are men. Hence,
$$\sum_{w=3}^{5}\binom{8}{w}\binom{10}{8-w}=\binom{8}{3}\binom{10}{5}+\binom{8}{4}\binom{10}{4}+\binom{8}{5}\binom{10}{3}=14,112+14,700+6,720=35,532.$$

questions.stem: For $f(x)=\dfrac{x^3-4x^2+x+6}{x-2}$ on $D=[-4,6]\setminus\{2\}$, which is the longest interval in $D$ on which $f$ is one-to-one?
questions.solution:
For $x\ne2$, $f(x)=x^2-2x-3$, so $f'(x)=2(x-1)$. Thus $f$ is strictly decreasing on $[-4,1]$, whose length is $5$; the other domain intervals on which it is one-to-one have lengths at most $4$.
Hence the longest interval is $[-4,1]$.

questions.stem: The mean of $12$ observations is $11$. If each observation $x$ is replaced by $6-2x$, what is the mean of the resulting observations?
questions.solution:
For the linear transformation $y=6-2x$, the mean transforms as $\bar y=6-2\bar x$.
$$\bar y=6-2(11)=-16$$

questions.stem: The sum of the coefficients of even powers of $x$ in the expansion of $(1+2x)^5(3-x)^4$ is
questions.solution:
For $P(x)=(1+2x)^5(3-x)^4$, the sum of coefficients of even powers is $4S_{\text{even}}=\dfrac{P(1)+P(-1)}{2}4$.
$$S_{\text{even}}=\frac{3^5\cdot2^4-4^4}{2}=\frac{3888-256}{2}=1816.$$

questions.stem: On reflecting the point $(4,3)$ in the line $x+2y-5=0$, its image is
questions.solution:
For reflection across $ax+by+c=0$, the image is $(x',y')=(x,y)-\dfrac{2(ax+by+c)}{a^2+b^2}(a,b)$. Thus
$$
(x',y')=(4,3)-\frac{2(4+2\cdot3-5)}{1^2+2^2}(1,2)=(2,-1).
$$
questions.subtopic: Image of a point in a line

questions.stem: Evaluate the definite integral $$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{1+x^2}{2+x^2+\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)^2}\,\frac{dx}{(1+\sin^2x)(1+\cos^2x)}.$$
questions.solution:
Under $x\mapsto \frac{\pi}{2}-x$, the rational factor averages with its complement to $\frac12$, so
$$I=\frac12\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{dx}{(1+\sin^2x)(1+\cos^2x)}.
$$
Setting $t=\tan x$ gives the integral on the right as $\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt2}$; hence $I=\boxed{\frac{\pi}{6\sqrt2}}$.

questions.stem: For what value of $k$ is $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^2+(k-2)x-2k}{x-2},&x<2,\\3x-k,&x\ge 2\end{cases}$ continuous at $x=2$?
questions.solution:
For $x<2$, factor the numerator:
$$\frac{(x-2)(x+k)}{x-2}=x+k,\qquad \lim_{x\to2^-}f(x)=2+k.$$
Since $f(2)=6-k$, continuity requires $2+k=6-k$, giving $k=2$.

questions.stem: For $f(x)=x^3+3x^2$, the maximal interval on which $f$ is decreasing is
questions.solution:
$$f'(x)=3x(x+2).$$
Since $f'(x)\le 0$ for $-2\le x\le 0$ and is positive outside this interval, $f$ is decreasing on the maximal interval $[-2,0]$.

questions.stem: The acute angle between the pair of lines represented by $x^2 + xy = 0$ is
questions.solution: The equation factors as $x(x+y)=0$, so the lines are $x=0$ and $x+y=0$. Their slopes are undefined and $-1$, respectively; hence the acute angle between them is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

questions.stem: A circle of radius $1$ is tangent to both lines $3x+4y=0$ and $3x+4y=10$. The locus of its centre is
questions.solution:
The centre is at distance $1$ from both lines, so
$$\frac{|3x+4y|}{5}=1,\qquad \frac{|3x+4y-10|}{5}=1.
$$
The common solution is $3x+4y=5$.

questions.stem: The domain of $f(x)=\sqrt{\dfrac{x^2-9}{x-1}}$ is
questions.solution: For the square root to be defined, require $\dfrac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-1}\ge 0$, with $x\ne1$. The critical points are $-3,1,3$; a sign chart gives $[-3,1)\cup[3,\infty)$.

questions.stem: The system $x+y+z=1$, $x+2y+2z=4$, $x+\lambda y+4z=10$ has infinitely many solutions when $\lambda$ is:
questions.solution: For infinitely many solutions, the third equation must be dependent on the first two. At $\lambda=4$, its left-hand side is $3$ times equation (2) minus $2$ times equation (1), and $3(4)-2(1)=10$ on the right-hand side as well. Thus the system is consistent with dependent equations, giving infinitely many solutions.

questions.stem: The general solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=1+\frac{y^2}{x^2}$ is
questions.solution:
Set $y=vx$, so $\frac{dy}{dx}=v+x\frac{dv}{dx}$.
$x\frac{dv}{dx}=v^2-v+1$.
$\frac{dv}{(v-\frac12)^2+\frac34}=\frac{dx}{x}$.
$\frac{2}{sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\frac{2v-1}{sqrt{3}}=ln|x|+C$.

questions.stem: A parabola has focus $(3,2)$ and directrix $x=-1$. What is its semi-latus rectum?
questions.solution: The vertex lies midway between the focus and directrix, so the focal distance is $a=\frac{4}{2}=2$. The semi-latus rectum of a parabola is $2a=2(2)=4$.

questions.stem: The foot $H$ of the perpendicular from $P=(2,1,1)$ to the plane $x+2y+2z=0$ is joined to $O=(0,0,0)$. Find $OH$.
questions.solution:
The foot of the perpendicular is the projection of $P$ onto the plane along its normal vector $(1,2,2)$.
$$H=P-\frac{P\boldsymbol{}(1,2,2)}{1^2+2^2+2^2}(1,2,2)=\left(\frac43,-\frac13,-\frac13\right)$$
Hence, $OH=\sqrt{\frac{16+1+1}{9}}=\sqrt2$.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^x(x^2+2x+1)\,dx$.
questions.solution:
Since $\frac{d}{dx}\left[e^x(x^2+1)\right]=e^x(x^2+2x+1)$,
$$\int_0^1 e^x(x^2+2x+1)\,dx=\left[e^x(x^2+1)\right]_0^1=2e-1.$$

questions.stem: Tangents from $P=(16,-4)$ touch the circle $x^2+y^2-6x+8y=0$ at $A$ and $B$. Find the perimeter of triangle $PAB$.
questions.solution:
The circle has centre $C=(3,-4)$ and radius $r=5$, while $PC=13$. Hence each tangent length is $PA=PB=\sqrt{PC^2-r^2}=12$.
The chord of contact is at distance $r^2/PC=25/13$ from $C$, so $AB=2\sqrt{5^2-(25/13)^2}=120/13$.
Thus the perimeter is $PA+PB+AB=24+120/13=\dfrac{432}{13}$.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \frac{3x+5}{(x+1)(x+2)}\,dx$.
questions.solution:
Resolve into partial fractions:
$$\frac{3x+5}{(x+1)(x+2)}=\frac{2}{x+1}+\frac{1}{x+2}.$$
Hence $\displaystyle\int_0^1\left(\frac{2}{x+1}+\frac{1}{x+2}\right)dx=\left[2\ln(x+1)+\ln(x+2)\right]_0^1=\ln 6$.

questions.stem: If $a$ and $b$ are arbitrary constants, the differential equation for the family $y=ax^2+bx$ is
questions.solution:
Differentiate the family: $y'=2ax+b$ and $y''=2a$. Substituting,
$$x^2y''-2xy'+2y=2ax^2-2x(2ax+b)+2(ax^2+bx)=0,$$
so the required differential equation is $x^2y''-2xy'+2y=0$.

questions.stem: The variance of a data set is $7$. What is the variance if each observation is multiplied by $3$ and then increased by $5$?
questions.solution:
For a linear transformation $Y=aX+b$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$; adding a constant does not affect variance.
$$\operatorname{Var}(Y)=3^2\times 7=63$$

questions.stem: For real $\theta$, which value is not in the range of $3\sin\theta+4\cos\theta+1$?
questions.solution:
The amplitude of $3\sin\theta+4\cos\theta$ is $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$, so
$$3\sin\theta+4\cos\theta+1\in[1-5,1+5]=[-4,6].$$
Hence $7$ is not in the range.

questions.stem:
For propositions $p$, $q$ and $r$, which statement is logically equivalent to $
eg[p\wedge(q\vee r)]$?

options.text:
$
eg p\wedge(
eg q\vee
eg r)$

$
eg p\vee(
eg q\wedge
eg r)$

$
eg p\vee(
eg q\vee
eg r)$

questions.solution:
By De Morgan’s laws,
$$
eg[p\wedge(q\vee r)]\equiv
eg p\vee
eg(q\vee r)\equiv
eg p\vee(
eg q\wedge
eg r).$$
Hence, the equivalent statement is (B).

questions.stem: If $\alpha,\beta$ are the roots of $3x^2-7x+2=0$, find $\alpha^2\beta+\alpha\beta^2$.
questions.solution:
By Vieta’s formulas, $\alpha+\beta=\frac{7}{3}$ and $\alpha\beta=\frac{2}{3}$. Hence
$$\alpha^2\beta+\alpha\beta^2=\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{7}{3}=\frac{14}{9}.$$

questions.stem: For $f(x)=2x^3-3x^2-12x+5$, the point of inflexion, where $f''$ changes sign, is
questions.solution:
The point of inflexion occurs where $f''(x)$ changes sign. Since
$$f''(x)=12x-6=0\Rightarrow x=\frac12,$$
and $f''$ changes sign there, $f\left(\frac12\right)=-\frac32$. Thus the point is $\left(\frac12,-\frac32\right)$.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\tan^{-1}\dfrac12+\tan^{-1}\dfrac13$.
questions.solution:
Let $A=\tan^{-1}\frac12$ and $B=\tan^{-1}\frac13$. Then
$$\tan(A+B)=\frac{\frac12+\frac13}{1-\frac16}=1.$$
Since $A,B>0$ and $A+B<\frac\pi2$, we get $A+B=\frac\pi4$.

questions.stem: The area enclosed by the parabolas $y=x^2$ and $y=2x$ is
questions.solution:
The curves intersect where $x^2=2x$, giving $x=0,2$. Between these points, $2x$ lies above $x^2$, so
$$A=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx=\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2=\frac{4}{3}.$$

questions.stem: A card is drawn from a standard deck. Let $A$ be the event that it is red and $B$ the event that it is a king. Given $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, $P(B)=\dfrac{1}{13}$ and $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{1}{26}$, find $P(A\cup B)$.
questions.solution:
By the addition rule of probability,
$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{13}-\frac{1}{26}=\frac{7}{13}.$$

questions.stem: Factories $A$ and $B$ produce all items. If $P(D\mid A)=\dfrac16$, $P(D\mid B)=\dfrac14$ and the total probability of a defect $D$ is $\dfrac15$, find $P(B\mid D)$.
questions.solution:
By Bayes’ theorem, first find $P(B)$. Let $P(B)=p$; then
$$\frac{1}{5}=\frac{1-p}{6}+\frac{p}{4}\quad\Rightarrow\quad p=\frac{2}{5}.$$
Hence $P(B\mid D)=\dfrac{P(D\mid B)P(B)}{P(D)}=\dfrac{(1/4)(2/5)}{1/5}=\dfrac{1}{2}.$

questions.stem: For $\sin\dfrac{d}{2}\ne0$, the sum $\cos\alpha+\cos(\alpha+d)+\cdots+\cos(\alpha+(n-1)d)$ is
questions.solution:
Using $2\sin\dfrac d2\cos(\alpha+kd)=\sin\left(\alpha+(k+\tfrac12)d\right)-\sin\left(\alpha+(k-\tfrac12)d\right)$, sum over $k=0,1,\ldots,n-1$; the sine terms telescope.
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos(\alpha+kd)=\frac{\sin\dfrac{nd}{2}}{\sin\dfrac d2}\cos\left(\alpha+\dfrac{(n-1)d}{2}\right)$$
Hence the expression is (C).

questions.stem: If $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j$, $\vec b=3\hat i-\hat j$ and $\vec c=7\hat i$, then the scalars $m,n$ satisfying $\vec c=m\vec a+n\vec b$ are
questions.solution:
Equating the coefficients of $\hat i$ and $\hat j$ gives
$$m+3n=7,\qquad 2m-n=0.$$
Thus $n=2m$, so $7m=7$ and $(m,n)=(1,2)$.

questions.stem: Two lines through the origin have direction vectors $(1,0,0)$ and $(3,4,12)$. What are the direction cosines of the bisector of the acute angle between the directed rays?
questions.solution:
The bisector of the acute angle between two directed rays is along the sum of their unit direction vectors.
$$\left(1,0,0\right)+\left(\frac3{13},\frac4{13},\frac{12}{13}\right)\propto(4,1,3),\qquad |(4,1,3)|=\sqrt{26}.$$
Hence its direction cosines are $\left(\frac4{\sqrt{26}},\frac1{\sqrt{26}},\frac3{\sqrt{26}}\right)$.

questions.stem: The position vectors of $A$, $B$ and $C$ are $(1,2,0)$, $(4,2,0)$ and $(1,6,0)$, respectively. The triangle $ABC$ is
questions.solution:
$overrightarrow{AB}=(3,0,0)$ and $overrightarrow{AC}=(0,4,0)$.
$$overrightarrow{AB}\cdotoverrightarrow{AC}=3(0)+0(4)+0(0)=0$$
Hence $AB\perp AC$, so the triangle is right-angled at $A$.

questions.stem: The radius of a sphere is increasing at $2$ cm min$^{-1}$. At the instant when its radius is $3$ cm, how fast is its volume increasing?
questions.solution:
The volume of a sphere is $V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, so
$$\frac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2\frac{dr}{dt}=4\pi(3)^2(2)=72\pi\text{ cm}^3\text{ min}^{-1}.$$

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$. Then $(I+A)^5$ is
questions.solution:
Since $A^2=A$, we have $(I+A)^n=I+(2^n-1)A$.
$$
(I+A)^5=I+31A=\begin{bmatrix}32&62\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
$$
